title: Using a Digital Thermometer to Perfectly Cook Steak Tartare on a Charcoal Grill
meta_description: Learn how to safely sear and prepare steak tartare using a charcoal grill and a digital thermometer for precision temperature and food safety.
html:
Steak tartare is typically known as a raw dish, but many gourmet chefs prefer a "seared tartare." This technique involves quickly charring the outside of a high-quality beef tenderloin on a high-heat grill to add a smoky dimension, then chilling and finely dicing the meat. To execute this without overcooking the interior, you need a digital thermometer steak tartare charcoal setup to ensure you hit the exact surface temperature without warming the core.

The Theory of the Seared Tartare

The goal here isn't to cook the steak to medium-rare. Instead, we are looking for a Maillard reaction—that deep, brown crust—on the very outer millimeter of the meat. This adds a layer of complexity that raw beef lacks, especially when using the primal heat of charcoal.

Because you are working with raw beef, precision is everything. If the heat penetrates too far, you've just made a rare steak, not tartare. This is where an Instant-Read Meat Thermometer becomes essential. You aren't monitoring the internal temperature for doneness; you are monitoring the surface and the rapid rise of heat to know exactly when to pull the meat off the grates.

Setting Up Your Charcoal Grill for Precision

For this method, you want a two-zone fire. Pile your glowing coals on one side of the grill to create a "nuclear" heat zone and leave the other side empty. This gives you a safety net; if the flare-ups become too intense, you can move the beef to the cool side immediately.

Before the meat hits the grill, pat it bone-dry with paper towels. Any moisture on the surface will create steam, which prevents the sear and increases the time the meat stays on the heat, risking the interior temperature. Season generously with salt and pepper just before placing it on the coals.

Using a Digital Thermometer for Steak Tartare on Charcoal

When searing for tartare, timing is measured in seconds, not minutes. Use your Instant-Read Meat Thermometer to check the surface of the meat. You are looking for a rapid spike in temperature on the exterior while ensuring the center remains cold (ideally around 38-40°F).

Follow these steps for the perfect sear:

  • Place the tenderloin on the hottest part of the charcoal grill.
  • Sear for roughly 30-45 seconds per side.
  • Use the thermometer to probe the very edge of the meat; you want to see a high surface temp, but the moment the probe sinks slightly deeper and the temp starts climbing toward 100°F, flip it.
  • Remove the beef the second the crust is formed.

The Chill and Dice Method

Once you've achieved that charcoal char, do not let the meat sit on a cutting board. The carry-over cooking will migrate toward the center, ruining the "raw" aspect of the tartare. Immediately wrap the seared beef in parchment paper and place it in the freezer for 10-15 minutes.

This flash-chill stops the cooking process instantly. Once chilled, use a very sharp knife to shave off the charred exterior into small cubes and mix them with the raw, chilled interior. This ensures every bite has a hint of charcoal smoke and a crunch of sear, while remaining safely chilled and tender.

Mixing and Serving Your Tartare

Now that your beef is prepped, combine the diced meat with traditional aromatics. I recommend a mix of capers, minced shallots, cornichons, and a touch of Dijon mustard. A drizzle of extra virgin olive oil and a squeeze of lemon juice will cut through the richness of the beef.

Since you used a digital thermometer steak tartare charcoal process, you can be confident in the temperature contrast of your dish. Serve it immediately with toasted sourdough or potato chips to complement the smoky notes from the grill.

FAQ

Is it safe to sear beef for tartare on a grill?

Yes, provided you use high-quality, sushi-grade or prime beef from a trusted butcher. The sear adds flavor and kills surface bacteria, but the safety of tartare depends primarily on the quality and freshness of the raw meat.

Why not just use a stovetop pan?

While a cast-iron skillet works, charcoal provides a distinct smoky flavor and a higher, more uneven heat that creates a more authentic "char" without cooking the meat through as quickly as a pan might.

Can I use a leave-in probe thermometer?

No. For this specific technique, a leave-in probe is too slow and bulky. You need an Instant-Read Meat Thermometer because the searing process happens so quickly that you need a reading in seconds to avoid overcooking the interior.
